title: MTH_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: f(x) = 3x² − 2x. Evaluate f(−2).
questions.why:
Square first, then multiply: 3(−2)² − 2(−2) = 3(4) + 4 = 12 + 4 = 16.

8 subtracts the 4 instead of adding it (12 − 4), losing the sign of −2(−2); −8 treats (−2)² as −4; 40 squares 3x instead of x, giving (3·(−2))² + 4.
questions.concept: Evaluating a quadratic at a negative input

questions.q: Find the domain of f(x) = (x + 4)/(x² − 7).
questions.why:
Set the denominator ≠ 0: x² − 7 ≠ 0, so x² ≠ 7 and x ≠ ±√7. Unlike x² + 7, this does have real solutions, so two values are removed: D = ℝ \ {−√7, √7}.

(−∞, ∞) treats x² − 7 as if it could never be zero, which is only true for x² + 7; ℝ \ {7} forgets to take the square root; ℝ \ {−4} excludes the zero of the numerator, which never restricts a domain.
questions.concept: Domain of a rational function with a real exclusion

questions.q: Find the range of f(x) = |x − 5| + 2.
questions.why:
|x − 5| ≥ 0, and adding 2 does not change the direction: |x − 5| + 2 ≥ 2, so y ≥ 2 and R = [2, ∞). The value 2 is attained at x = 5.

(−∞, 2] reverses the inequality even though nothing was multiplied by a negative; [5, ∞) reads the 5 inside the absolute value as an output bound; [−2, ∞) has the sign of the constant wrong.
questions.concept: Range of an absolute value function

questions.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = (x − 4)/3.
questions.why:
Let y = (x − 4)/3. Switch: x = (y − 4)/3. Isolate y: 3x = y − 4, so y = 3x + 4. Check: f(10) = 2 and f⁻¹(2) = 10.

3x − 4 undoes the division but moves the 4 with the wrong sign; (x + 4)/3 changes a sign without ever switching x and y, so it is not an inverse; 3/(x − 4) is the reciprocal, not the inverse.
questions.concept: Inverse of a linear function

questions.q: f(x) = x² + 2 and g(x) = 4x − 1. Find (f ∘ g)(x) in expanded form.
questions.why:
f ∘ g = f[g(x)] = (4x − 1)² + 2 = (4x − 1)(4x − 1) + 2 = 16x² − 4x − 4x + 1 + 2 = 16x² − 8x + 3.

16x² + 3 squares term by term and loses the −8x cross term; 4x² + 7 is g ∘ f = 4(x² + 2) − 1, the wrong order; 16x² − 8x + 1 expands the square but forgets the + 2.
questions.concept: Expanding a squared composite

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 3 and g(x) = 2x + 1. Evaluate (g ∘ f)(2).
questions.why:
g ∘ f means f runs first: f(2) = 2² − 3 = 1, then g(1) = 2(1) + 1 = 3.

22 is (f ∘ g)(2), the wrong order (g(2) = 5, then f(5) = 22); 5 stops at g(2); 1 stops at f(2).
questions.concept: Evaluating a composite at a number

questions.q: Find the range of h(x) = 5 − √(x − 1).
questions.why:
√(x − 1) ≥ 0. Multiplying by −1 reverses it: −√(x − 1) ≤ 0. Adding 5 does not: 5 − √(x − 1) ≤ 5, so R = (−∞, 5]. The value 5 is attained at x = 1.

[5, ∞) forgets that multiplying by −1 flips the inequality; [1, ∞) is the domain, not the range; (−∞, 1] mixes the domain endpoint into the range.
questions.concept: Range of a square root function

questions.q: A function f satisfies f(3) = 11. What is f⁻¹(11)?
questions.why:
The inverse sends each output back to its input: f takes 3 to 11, so f⁻¹ takes 11 back to 3. No formula for f is needed.

1/11 is the reciprocal of 11, which is 1/f(3) and not an inverse; 11 confuses the input of f⁻¹ with its output; 1/3 is the reciprocal of the answer.
questions.concept: Meaning of an inverse function

questions.q: Find the equation of the straight line through (2, −1) and (5, 8).
questions.why:
m = (8 − (−1))/(5 − 2) = 9/3 = 3. Then y − (−1) = 3(x − 2), so y + 1 = 3x − 6 and y = 3x − 7. Check: 3(5) − 7 = 8.

y = 3x + 5 has the right slope but computes the intercept as y₁ + mx₁ = −1 + 6 instead of y₁ − mx₁ = −1 − 6; (1/3)x − 5/3 inverts the slope as Δx/Δy = 3/9; −3x + 5 has the sign of the slope wrong.
questions.concept: Equation of a line through two points

questions.q: Find the vertex of f(x) = 2x² + 8x − 1.
questions.why:
x = −b/2a = −8/4 = −2, and f(−2) = 2(4) − 16 − 1 = −9, so the vertex is (−2, −9).

(−2, −1) takes the constant c as the vertex height, but c is the y-intercept f(0); (2, 23) drops the minus sign in −b/2a; (−4, −1) uses −b/a instead of −b/2a.
questions.concept: Vertex of a quadratic

questions.q: Solve 4 · 5ˣ = 500.
questions.why:
Isolate the power first: 5ˣ = 500/4 = 125. Since 125 = 5³, x = 3.

x = 125 stops after dividing and forgets to take the logarithm; x = 4 divides 500 by 125 instead of recognising 125 as 5³; x = 2 gives 5² = 25, one power short.
questions.concept: Solving an exponential equation

questions.q: Evaluate log₂ (1/8).
questions.why:
log₂ (1/8) asks: 2 to what power is 1/8? Since 1/8 = 2⁻³, the answer is −3.

3 forgets that a fraction between 0 and 1 needs a negative exponent; −4 gives 2⁻⁴ = 1/16, one power off; 1/3 takes the reciprocal of the exponent instead of its negative.
questions.concept: Evaluating a logarithm

questions.q: Solve |x + 2| ≤ 5. Give the answer as an interval.
questions.why:
Unfold the absolute value: −5 ≤ x + 2 ≤ 5. Subtract 2 throughout: −7 ≤ x ≤ 3, so the solution is [−7, 3].

[−3, 7] adds 2 instead of subtracting; (−∞, −7] ∪ [3, ∞) is the solution of |x + 2| ≥ 5, the outside of the interval; [3, 7] keeps the two endpoints without their signs and is not a solution set at all.
questions.concept: Solving an absolute value inequality

questions.q: f(x) = 2x − 1 if x < 3, and f(x) = x² − 5 if x ≥ 3. Find f(3) − f(−1).
questions.why:
x = 3 satisfies x ≥ 3, so f(3) = 3² − 5 = 4. x = −1 satisfies x < 3, so f(−1) = 2(−1) − 1 = −3. Then f(3) − f(−1) = 4 − (−3) = 7.

8 uses the wrong branch for one of the inputs (f(3) = 5 from 2x − 1, or f(−1) = −4 from x² − 5); 1 adds instead of subtracting, 4 + (−3); 9 uses the wrong branch for both inputs, 5 − (−4).
questions.concept: Evaluating a piecewise function

questions.q: f(x) = 4 − 3x⁵ + x². What does f(x) do as x → −∞?
questions.why:
For large |x| the leading term −3x⁵ decides everything. Degree 5 is odd, so x⁵ → −∞ as x → −∞, and the negative coefficient flips it: −3x⁵ → +∞. So f(x) → +∞.

−∞ ignores the sign of the leading coefficient and reports where x⁵ alone goes; 4 treats the constant term as the value far out; −3 reads the leading coefficient itself as the limit, but the coefficient only fixes the direction, not a finite height.
questions.concept: End behaviour from the leading term

questions.q: The circle x² + y² = 9 does not define y as a function of x. Which test shows this?
options: The horizontal line y = 1 cuts it twice
The vertical line x = 1 cuts it twice
The equation is not a polynomial
questions.why:
A graph is a function of x only if every vertical line meets it at most once. At x = 1 the circle has y = √8 and y = −√8, two outputs for one input, so the vertical line test fails.

A horizontal line cutting twice tests whether a function is one-to-one, not whether it is a function; the circle does have y-intercepts, (0, 3) and (0, −3); not being a polynomial is irrelevant, since √x and |x| are functions too.
questions.concept: Vertical line test

questions.q: Which of these is an exponential function?
questions.why:
An exponential function has the variable in the exponent and a constant base: f(x) = a·bˣ with b > 0, b ≠ 1. Only 3ˣ has that shape.

x³ has the variable in the base, so it is a power (polynomial) function; 3x is linear; x^(1/3) is a root, again a power of x.
questions.concept: Exponential versus power function

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→−1) (x³ + 2)/(x² + 3).
questions.why:
Substitute x = −1: ((−1)³ + 2)/((−1)² + 3) = (−1 + 2)/(1 + 3) = 1/4. The denominator is not zero, so direct substitution is the whole method.

3/4 treats (−1)³ as +1; 1/2 treats (−1)² as −1 in the denominator; DNE is wrong because the expression is well defined at x = −1.
questions.concept: Limit by direct substitution

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→−3) (x² − 9)/(x + 3).
questions.why:
Substitution gives (9 − 9)/(−3 + 3) = 0/0, so factor: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). Cancel the (x + 3): lim(x→−3) (x − 3) = −3 − 3 = −6.

6 has the sign wrong, evaluating x − 3 at x = 3 instead of x = −3; 0 reads the 0 in the numerator as the answer; DNE treats 0/0 as a verdict instead of a signal to factor.
questions.concept: Limit by factoring and cancelling

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x² − x − 2)/(x² − 4).
questions.why:
Substitution gives 0/0. Factor both: x² − x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1) and x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2). Cancel (x − 2): lim(x→2) (x + 1)/(x + 2) = 3/4.

DNE stops at the 0/0 form; 1/4 mis-factors the numerator as (x − 2)(x − 1); 3/2 evaluates (x + 1)/(x + 2) with the x dropped from the denominator, (2 + 1)/2.
questions.concept: Limit with two factorable quadratics

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (1/x − 1/3)/(x − 3).
questions.why:
Multiply top and bottom by the common denominator 3x: the numerator becomes 3 − x and the denominator 3x(x − 3). Write 3 − x = −1(x − 3) and cancel: lim(x→3) −1/(3x) = −1/9.

1/9 cancels 3 − x against x − 3 without the −1; −1/3 forgets the factor x in the denominator 3x; −1/6 substitutes into −1/(x + 3) instead of −1/(3x).
questions.concept: Limit of a complex fraction

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(x + 25) − 5)/x.
questions.why:
Multiply by the conjugate (√(x + 25) + 5) over itself: the numerator becomes (x + 25) − 25 = x, which cancels the x below, leaving lim(x→0) 1/(√(x + 25) + 5) = 1/(5 + 5) = 1/10.

0 substitutes into the numerator only and ignores the 0 below; 1/5 forgets to add the second 5 from the conjugate; 10 is the reciprocal of the answer.
questions.concept: Limit by rationalising the numerator

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→25) (x − 25)/(√x − 5).
questions.why:
Substitution gives 0/0. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √x + 5: the denominator becomes x − 25, which cancels with the numerator, leaving lim(x→25) (√x + 5) = 5 + 5 = 10.

1/10 is the reciprocal, the answer to the upside-down limit (√x − 5)/(x − 25); 5 takes √25 alone and forgets the + 5; 0 reads the 0 in the numerator as the answer.
questions.concept: Limit with a root in the denominator

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (e^(2x) − 1)/(sin x).
questions.why:
Substitution gives (1 − 1)/0 = 0/0, so apply L'Hôpital's Rule: f(x) = e^(2x) − 1, g(x) = sin x, f′(x) = 2e^(2x), g′(x) = cos x. Then lim(x→0) 2e^(2x)/cos x = 2(1)/1 = 2.

1 forgets the chain-rule factor 2 when differentiating e^(2x); 0 substitutes into the numerator only; DNE treats 0/0 as a verdict.
questions.concept: Limit by L'Hôpital's Rule

questions.q: lim(x→c) f(x) = 6 and lim(x→c) g(x) = −2. Find lim(x→c) [f(x)/g(x) + g(x)²].
questions.why:
By the quotient property (allowed since lim g ≠ 0), lim f/g = 6/(−2) = −3. By the power property, lim g² = (−2)² = 4. By the sum property the total is −3 + 4 = 1.

−7 squares −2 as −4; 7 loses the sign of the quotient, 3 + 4; −5 forgets to square, −3 + (−2).
questions.concept: Combining limit properties

questions.q: When may L'Hôpital's Rule be applied to lim(x→c) f(x)/g(x)?
options: Whenever the denominator is a polynomial
Whenever the limit is at infinity
Whenever f and g are both differentiable
questions.why:
L'Hôpital's Rule replaces f/g by f′/g′ only when substitution produces an indeterminate form, 0/0 or ∞/∞. Applied to a quotient that is already well defined it gives a wrong answer: lim(x→1) (x + 1)/x is 2, but differentiating top and bottom gives 1/1 = 1.

The form of the denominator and the location of c do not matter; differentiability is needed but is not enough, as the (x + 1)/x example shows.
questions.concept: Condition for L'Hôpital's Rule

questions.q: For x < 4 a curve rises to an open circle at (4, 6). For x > 4 the curve starts at an open circle at (4, 1) and continues. A solid dot sits at (4, 3). Find lim(x→4) f(x).
questions.why:
lim(x→4⁻) f(x) = 6, the height the left branch runs into, and lim(x→4⁺) f(x) = 1, where the right branch starts. The one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist: DNE. The solid dot gives f(4) = 3, which is not the limit.

6 and 1 are the one-sided limits, not the two-sided one; 3 is f(4), the value at the point, which the limit never inspects.
questions.concept: Two-sided limit from a described graph

questions.q: Both branches of a curve run into an open circle at (−2, 5), and a solid dot sits at (−2, 1). State lim(x→−2) f(x) and f(−2).
questions.why:
Both sides approach height 5, so lim(x→−2) f(x) = 5. The function value is the solid dot: f(−2) = 1. The limit exists but does not equal f(−2), so this is a removable discontinuity.

lim = 1, f(−2) = 5 swaps the roles of the open circle and the solid dot; DNE is wrong because the one-sided limits agree; f(−2) = 5 reads the open circle as a function value, which it never is.
questions.concept: Limit versus function value on a graph

questions.q: f(x) = (x² − 16)/(x − 4). Find lim(x→4) f(x) and name the discontinuity at x = 4.
questions.why:
Substitution gives 0/0. Factor: (x − 4)(x + 4)/(x − 4) = x + 4 for x ≠ 4, so lim(x→4) f(x) = 8. f(4) itself is 0/0, undefined, so condition (i) fails: the limit exists but the point is missing, a removable discontinuity (a hole at (4, 8)).

DNE; jump needs unequal one-sided limits, but both are 8; continuous is wrong because f(4) is undefined; infinite needs a vertical asymptote, and the graph is just the line y = x + 4 with a hole.
questions.concept: Removable discontinuity by factoring

questions.q: f(x) = 3x + k for x ≤ 2, and f(x) = x² + 1 for x > 2. Find k so that f is continuous at x = 2.
questions.why:
Left: lim(x→2⁻) (3x + k) = 6 + k, which is also f(2). Right: lim(x→2⁺) (x² + 1) = 5. Continuity needs 6 + k = 5, so k = −1.

1 has the sign wrong (solves 6 − k = 5); 11 adds 6 and 5 instead of subtracting; 5 is the right-hand limit, not k.
questions.concept: Choosing a constant for continuity

questions.q: Find lim(x→−1⁻) 3/(x + 1).
questions.why:
As x → −1 from the left, x is slightly less than −1, so x + 1 is a small negative number, and 3 divided by a small negative number is a large negative number: the limit is −∞ (an infinite discontinuity at x = −1).

+∞ takes the approach from the right, where x + 1 is small and positive; 0 and 3 come from substituting into the numerator and ignoring the denominator.
questions.concept: One-sided infinite limit

questions.q: g(x) = (x² − 5x + 6)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3, and g(3) = 2. Which continuity condition fails at x = 3?
questions.why:
Factor: (x − 2)(x − 3)/(x − 3) = x − 2 for x ≠ 3, so lim(x→3) g(x) = 1. g(3) = 2 is defined (condition i holds) and the limit exists (ii holds), but 1 ≠ 2, so condition (iii) fails and g has a removable discontinuity at 3.

(i) is wrong because g(3) is given as 2; (ii) is wrong because both one-sided limits are 1; g would be continuous only if g(3) were redefined as 1.
questions.concept: Three conditions for continuity at a point

questions.q: Which set of readings describes a jump discontinuity at x = c?
questions.why:
A jump has both one-sided limits finite but unequal: 2 ≠ −1. The value f(c) may be either of them, or neither, and does not change the classification.

Equal one-sided limits of 2 with f(c) = 5 is a removable discontinuity (a hole with the dot in the wrong place); +∞ on both sides is an infinite discontinuity (vertical asymptote); limits and value all equal to 2 is continuity, not a discontinuity.
questions.concept: Classifying a discontinuity from one-sided limits

questions.q: The graph of f(x) = |x − 2| is a V shape with a sharp corner at (2, 0). At x = 2, f is
questions.why:
Continuity has nothing to do with smoothness: lim(x→2⁻) |x − 2| = 0, lim(x→2⁺) |x − 2| = 0 and f(2) = 0, so all three conditions hold and f is continuous at 2. The pen never lifts at a corner.

A jump needs unequal one-sided limits; removable needs the limit to differ from f(2) or f(2) to be missing; essential needs a one-sided limit that fails to exist. None of that happens here.
questions.concept: Corner versus discontinuity

questions.q: Differentiate f(x) = 4x⁶ − 3x² + 9x − 2.
questions.why:
Power rule term by term: 4x⁶ → 24x⁵, −3x² → −6x, 9x → 9 (since x⁰ = 1), −2 → 0. f′(x) = 24x⁵ − 6x + 9.

24x⁵ − 6x + 9x leaves the x on the linear term instead of reducing it to 9x⁰ = 9; 4x⁵ − 3x + 9 drops each power without multiplying by it; 24x⁵ − 6x + 7 keeps the constant −2 instead of sending it to 0.
questions.concept: Power rule on a polynomial

questions.q: Find f′(x) for f(x) = x³ cos x.
questions.why:
Product rule with u = x³, v = cos x, u′ = 3x², v′ = −sin x: f′(x) = u v′ + u′ v = x³(−sin x) + 3x² cos x = 3x² cos x − x³ sin x.

3x² cos x + x³ sin x forgets the minus in d/dx(cos x) = −sin x; −3x² sin x is u′v′, differentiating both factors and multiplying; 3x² cos x differentiates only the x³ and leaves cos x alone.
questions.concept: Product rule with a trigonometric factor

questions.q: Find f′(x) for f(x) = (2x + 3)/(x − 1).
questions.why:
Quotient rule with u = 2x + 3, v = x − 1, u′ = 2, v′ = 1: f′(x) = [v u′ − u v′]/v² = [(x − 1)(2) − (2x + 3)(1)]/(x − 1)² = (2x − 2 − 2x − 3)/(x − 1)² = −5/(x − 1)².

5/(x − 1)² swaps the two numerator terms, which flips the sign; −5/(x − 1) forgets to square the denominator; (4x + 1)/(x − 1)² adds the two products instead of subtracting.
questions.concept: Quotient rule

questions.q: Find f′(x) for f(x) = (x² + 5)⁴.
questions.why:
Chain rule with u = x² + 5, y = u⁴: y′(u) = 4u³, u′(x) = 2x, so f′(x) = 4u³ · 2x = 8x(x² + 5)³.

4(x² + 5)³ forgets the inner derivative 2x; 8x(x² + 5)⁴ does not reduce the power; 4(2x)³ differentiates the inside first and then raises it to the power, which no rule allows.
questions.concept: Chain rule with a power

questions.q: Differentiate x² + xy − y² = 5 implicitly and make dy/dx the subject.
questions.why:
Differentiate each term with respect to x: 2x + (y + x dy/dx) − 2y dy/dx = 0, using the product rule on xy and the chain rule on y². Collect: dy/dx (x − 2y) = −(2x + y), so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x − 2y) = (2x + y)/(2y − x).

(2x + y)/(x − 2y) drops the minus sign when dividing; x/y forgets the xy term entirely and solves 2x − 2y dy/dx = 0; 2x/(2y − x) differentiates xy as x dy/dx only, missing the y from the product rule.
questions.concept: Implicit differentiation with a product term

questions.q: A curve is given by x = 4t − 1 and y = t³ + 2t. Find dy/dx.
questions.why:
dx/dt = 4 and dy/dt = 3t² + 2. The parametric rule is dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt) = (3t² + 2)/4, and the answer stays in terms of t.

4/(3t² + 2) divides the wrong way round; 3t² + 2 is dy/dt alone, not the gradient; (3t² + 2)/(4t − 1) divides by x instead of by dx/dt.
questions.concept: Parametric differentiation

questions.q: f(x, y) = 5x²y − 4y³ + 2x. Find ∂f/∂y.
questions.why:
Treat x as a constant: 5x²y → 5x², −4y³ → −12y², 2x → 0 (no y in it). ∂f/∂y = 5x² − 12y².

10xy + 2 is ∂f/∂x, treating y as the constant; 5x² − 12y² + 2 differentiates 2x as if it contained y; 10xy − 12y² mixes the two partials, differentiating the first term by x and the second by y.
questions.concept: Partial derivative treating one variable as constant

questions.q: y is a function of x. In implicit differentiation, d/dx(y³) equals
questions.why:
y³ is a composite: the outside u³ differentiates to 3u² = 3y², and the chain rule owes the inner derivative dy/dx, giving 3y² dy/dx.

3y² is d/dy(y³), differentiating with respect to the wrong variable; 3x² dy/dx replaces y by x for no reason; 0 would be right only if y were a constant, which in implicit differentiation it is not (that is the partial-derivative setting).
questions.concept: Chain rule factor in implicit differentiation

questions.q: f(x) = 2x⁴ − 5x³ + x − 8. Find f″(x).
questions.why:
f′(x) = 8x³ − 15x² + 1. Differentiate again: f″(x) = 24x² − 30x + 0 = 24x² − 30x.

8x³ − 15x² + 1 stops at the first derivative; 24x² − 30x + 1 keeps the constant 1, whose derivative is 0; 48x − 30 goes one order too far, to f‴(x).
questions.concept: Second derivative of a polynomial

questions.q: y = √x. Find d²y/dx².
questions.why:
Write y = x^(1/2). Then y′ = (1/2)x^(−1/2), and y″ = (1/2)(−1/2)x^(−1/2 − 1) = −(1/4)x^(−3/2), which is −1/(4x√x).

(1/4)x^(−3/2) loses the minus that comes from the exponent −1/2; −(1/2)x^(−3/2) forgets to multiply the two coefficients; −(1/4)x^(−1/2) does not lower the exponent by 1 at the second step.
questions.concept: Second derivative with a fractional power

questions.q: y = e^(−3x). Find y⁽⁴⁾.
questions.why:
Each differentiation multiplies by the chain factor −3: y′ = −3e^(−3x), y″ = 9e^(−3x), y‴ = −27e^(−3x), y⁽⁴⁾ = 81e^(−3x). Four factors of −3 give (−3)⁴ = 81, positive.

−81e^(−3x) miscounts the sign (an even number of factors −3 is positive); −27e^(−3x) is the third derivative; 12e^(−3x) adds 3 four times instead of multiplying.
questions.concept: Higher derivatives of an exponential

questions.q: y = cos(4x). Find y‴.
questions.why:
Chain factor 4 each time: y′ = −4 sin(4x), y″ = −16 cos(4x), y‴ = −16 · (−4 sin(4x)) = 64 sin(4x).

−64 sin(4x) loses one of the two sign changes (cos → −sin happens at steps 1 and 3); 4 sin(4x) forgets that the factor 4 appears at every step; 64 cos(4x) is the wrong function, since sin and cos alternate at each order.
questions.concept: Higher derivatives of a trigonometric function

questions.q: f(x) = ln(2x + 1). Find f″(x).
questions.why:
Chain rule: f′(x) = 2/(2x + 1) = 2(2x + 1)⁻¹. Differentiate again: f″(x) = 2 · (−1)(2x + 1)⁻² · 2 = −4/(2x + 1)².

4/(2x + 1)² loses the minus from the exponent −1; −2/(2x + 1)² forgets the chain factor 2 at the second step; −1/(2x + 1)² forgets it at both steps.
questions.concept: Second derivative of a logarithm

questions.q: f(x) = x²eˣ. Find f″(x).
questions.why:
Product rule at each order. f′(x) = 2x eˣ + x² eˣ = (x² + 2x)eˣ. Then f″(x) = (2x + 2)eˣ + (x² + 2x)eˣ = (x² + 4x + 2)eˣ.

(x² + 2x)eˣ stops at the first derivative; (x² + 2)eˣ drops the 4x when collecting 2x + 2x; (x² + 4x)eˣ drops the constant 2 that comes from differentiating 2x.
questions.concept: Second derivative by the product rule

questions.q: f(x) = x⁴ − 2x². Find f‴(1).
questions.why:
f′(x) = 4x³ − 4x, f″(x) = 12x² − 4, f‴(x) = 24x. So f‴(1) = 24.

8 is f″(1) = 12 − 4; 0 is f′(1) = 4 − 4; 12 comes from differentiating 12x² − 4 to 12 without the x.
questions.concept: Evaluating a third derivative at a point

questions.q: The position s(t) of a car is differentiated three times. What does d³s/dt³ represent?
questions.why:
The first derivative of position is velocity, the second is acceleration (how velocity changes), and the third is jerk (how acceleration changes).

Velocity is ds/dt; acceleration is d²s/dt²; distance is the position itself, before any differentiation.
questions.concept: Physical meaning of higher derivatives

questions.q: Find ∫(4x³ − 6x + 5) dx.
questions.why:
Integrate term by term with ∫xⁿdx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c: 4x³ gives 4x⁴/4 = x⁴, 6x gives 6x²/2 = 3x², and 5 gives 5x by the rule with n = 0. So the answer is x⁴ − 3x² + 5x + c.

12x² − 6 differentiates instead of integrating; 4x⁴ − 6x² + 5x raises each power but never divides by the new power; x⁴ − 3x² + 5 leaves the constant term as 5 instead of 5x.
questions.concept: Integrating a polynomial term by term

questions.q: Find ∫(3/x⁵) dx.
questions.why:
Rewrite the fraction as a power first: 3/x⁵ = 3x⁻⁵, so n = −5 and n + 1 = −4. Then ∫3x⁻⁵dx = 3x⁻⁴/(−4) + c = −3/(4x⁴) + c. Check by differentiating: (−3/4)(−4)x⁻⁵ = 3x⁻⁵.

3/(4x⁴) loses the minus that dividing by −4 produces; −3/(6x⁶) lowers the power to −6 instead of raising it to −4; −1/(4x⁴) drops the coefficient 3.
questions.concept: Power rule with a negative exponent

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an antiderivative of 6x²?
questions.why:
An antiderivative F satisfies F′(x) = 6x². Differentiating 6x³ gives 18x², not 6x², so it is not one. The family of antiderivatives is 2x³ + c, since (2x³)′ = 6x² and the derivative of any constant is 0.

2x³ + 5, 2x³ and 2x³ − 9 all differentiate to 6x², which is exactly why the constant of integration has to be written: the antiderivative is never unique.
questions.concept: Antiderivatives and the constant of integration

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁⁴ x√x dx by first writing x√x as a power of x.
questions.why:
x√x = x·x^(1/2) = x^(3/2), so n = 3/2 and F(x) = x^(5/2)/(5/2) = (2/5)x^(5/2). Then F(4) − F(1) = (2/5)(32) − (2/5)(1) = 64/5 − 2/5 = 62/5.

64/5 forgets to subtract the value at the lower limit; 14/3 integrates √x alone, giving (2/3)(8 − 1); 31/5 halves the correct answer by using x^(5/2)/5.
questions.concept: Rewriting a root as a power before integrating

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁² (3x² − 4x) dx.
questions.why:
F(x) = x³ − 2x². Then F(2) = 8 − 8 = 0 and F(−1) = −1 − 2 = −3, so the integral is F(2) − F(−1) = 0 − (−3) = 3. Subtracting a negative adds.

1 comes from taking (−1)³ = +1; −3 reverses the order to F(−1) − F(2); 0 forgets the lower limit altogether and reports F(2).
questions.concept: Definite integral with a negative lower limit

questions.q: F′(x) = 6x² − 2 and F(2) = 5. Find F(x).
questions.why:
Integrate: F(x) = ∫(6x² − 2)dx = 2x³ − 2x + C. Now use the data point: F(2) = 16 − 4 + C = 12 + C, and 12 + C = 5 gives C = −7. So F(x) = 2x³ − 2x − 7.

2x³ − 2x + 5 copies the given value straight into C instead of solving for it; 6x³ − 2x − 7 fails to divide 6 by the new power 3; 2x³ − 2x + 17 solves 12 + C = 5 with a sign slip.
questions.concept: Finding the constant of integration from a data point

questions.q: Find the number a > 0 for which ∫₁ᵃ 4x³ dx = 80.
questions.why:
∫4x³dx = x⁴, so ∫₁ᵃ4x³dx = a⁴ − 1. Setting a⁴ − 1 = 80 gives a⁴ = 81, and the positive fourth root is a = 3.

a = 2 solves a⁴ − 1 = 15; a = 20 divides 80 by 4 and ignores the power; a = 81 stops at a⁴ = 81 and forgets to take the fourth root.
questions.concept: Solving for a limit of integration

questions.q: f is continuous on [a, b] and F′(x) = f(x). Which expression equals ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx?
options: f(b) − f(a), using the integrand itself
questions.why:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a), upper limit first.

f(b) − f(a) substitutes into the integrand rather than the antiderivative; F(a) − F(b) reverses the order and flips the sign of the answer; F(b) − F(a) + c adds a constant that always cancels, since (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a), so a definite integral never carries one.
questions.concept: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

questions.q: Find ∫sin(5x) dx.
questions.why:
Put u = 5x, so du = 5dx and dx = du/5. Then ∫sin(u)du/5 = −cos(u)/5 + C = −cos(5x)/5 + C. Check: d/dx[−cos(5x)/5] = sin(5x)·5/5 = sin(5x).

−5cos(5x) multiplies by 5 instead of dividing; cos(5x)/5 loses the minus in ∫sin = −cos; −cos(5x) forgets the inner derivative altogether.
questions.concept: Integrating sin(kx) by substitution

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ (2x + 3)⁴ dx using the substitution u = 2x + 3.
questions.why:
u = 2x + 3 gives du = 2dx, so dx = du/2, and the limits convert: x = 0 gives u = 3, x = 1 gives u = 5. So the integral is (1/2)∫₃⁵u⁴du = (1/10)[u⁵]₃⁵ = (3125 − 243)/10 = 2882/10 = 1441/5.

2882/5 omits the factor 1/2 from dx = du/2; 625/2 drops the value at the lower limit; 1/10 keeps the old limits 0 and 1 instead of converting them to u.
questions.concept: Definite integral by substitution with converted limits

questions.q: Find ∫x·sin(2x) dx.
questions.why:
Use ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du with u = x and dv = sin(2x)dx, so du = dx and v = −cos(2x)/2. Then ∫x·sin(2x)dx = −x·cos(2x)/2 + (1/2)∫cos(2x)dx = −x·cos(2x)/2 + sin(2x)/4 + C.

sin(2x)/2 forgets the second inner derivative when integrating cos(2x); x·cos(2x)/2 − sin(2x)/4 takes v = cos(2x)/2 and loses the minus in ∫sin = −cos; the last option multiplies by 2 where the substitution divides.
questions.concept: Integration by parts with a trigonometric factor

questions.q: Find ∫x²·ln(x) dx.
questions.why:
Take u = ln(x) and dv = x²dx, since x² is easy to integrate and ln(x) becomes simple when differentiated: du = dx/x and v = x³/3. Then ∫x²ln(x)dx = (x³/3)ln(x) − ∫(x³/3)(1/x)dx = (x³/3)ln(x) − (1/3)(x³/3) = (x³/3)ln(x) − x³/9 + C.

−x³/3 forgets to divide the leftover ∫x²dx/3 by 3 again; +x³/9 loses the minus sign of the parts formula; the last option multiplies the two separate integrals, which parts never licenses.
questions.concept: Integration by parts with a logarithm

questions.q: Find ∫(3x + 11)/((x − 3)(x + 2)) dx by partial fractions.
questions.why:
Write (3x + 11)/((x − 3)(x + 2)) = A/(x − 3) + B/(x + 2) and clear denominators: 3x + 11 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 3). At x = 3, 20 = 5A so A = 4; at x = −2, 5 = −5B so B = −1. Then the integral is ∫[4/(x − 3) − 1/(x + 2)]dx = 4ln(x − 3) − ln(x + 2) + C.

The first option keeps B positive; the third swaps A and B; the fourth attaches each constant to the wrong factor.
questions.concept: Partial fractions with distinct linear factors

questions.q: Find ∫2x/(x² + 1) dx.
questions.why:
Put u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx and the whole numerator is swallowed: ∫du/u = ln(u) + C = ln(x² + 1) + C. Check by differentiating: 2x/(x² + 1).

(1/2)ln(x² + 1) divides by 2 as though du = x dx; 2ln(x² + 1) pulls the 2 out and then uses it again; 2x·ln(x² + 1) treats the variable factor 2x as a constant that can be moved outside the integral.
questions.concept: Substitution giving a logarithm

questions.q: Find ∫√(4 − x²) dx using the substitution x = 2sin(u).
questions.why:
With x = 2sin(u), dx = 2cos(u)du and √(4 − x²) = √(4cos²(u)) = 2cos(u), so the integral becomes 4∫cos²(u)du. Using cos²(u) = (1 + cos(2u))/2 gives 2u + sin(2u), and sin(2u) = 2sin(u)cos(u) = 2(x/2)(√(4 − x²)/2). Setting back u = sin⁻¹(x/2) gives 2sin⁻¹(x/2) + x√(4 − x²)/2 + C.

The second option loses one of the two factors of 2 in 4∫cos²(u)du; the third mishandles sin(2u)/2 when returning to x; the fourth has the wrong sign on the second term.
questions.concept: Trigonometric substitution for √(a² − x²)

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) cos²(x) dx using cos²(x) = (1 + cos(2x))/2.
questions.why:
∫cos²(x)dx = x/2 + sin(2x)/4. At x = π/2 this is π/4 + sin(π)/4 = π/4, and at x = 0 it is 0, so the value is π/4.

π/2 integrates 1 + cos(2x) without halving it; 1 integrates cos(x) instead of cos²(x); π/4 + 1/2 uses sin(x)/2 in place of sin(2x)/4 and picks up a spurious 1/2 at the upper limit.
questions.concept: Definite integral of cos² using the double-angle identity

questions.q: Which first move evaluates ∫2x/(x² + 5)³ dx?
options: Integration by parts with u = 2x and dv = (x² + 5)⁻³dx
questions.why:
Substitution works when an inner function and its derivative both appear. Here the inner function is x² + 5 and its derivative 2x is exactly the numerator, so u = x² + 5, du = 2x dx turns the integral into ∫u⁻³du = −1/(2u²) + C.

Parts needs dv to be something you can integrate, and (x² + 5)⁻³ is not; partial fractions needs a factorable denominator of separate linear factors, and x² + 5 has none; the tangent substitution is for a root or a first power of x² + a², and it makes this integral harder, not easier.
questions.concept: Choosing an integration technique

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁^∞ x^(−5/2) dx.
questions.why:
Write the limit first: lim(t→∞)∫₁ᵗ x^(−5/2)dx = lim(t→∞)[−(2/3)x^(−3/2)]₁ᵗ = lim(t→∞)[−2/(3t^(3/2)) + 2/3] = 2/3, so the integral converges to 2/3.

3/2 gives the reciprocal of the coefficient; 2/5 divides by the original power 5/2 instead of the new power 3/2; the integral is not divergent, since p = 5/2 > 1.
questions.concept: Type I improper integral of a power

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ e^(−3x) dx.
questions.why:
∫₀^∞e^(−3x)dx = lim(t→∞)[−e^(−3x)/3]₀ᵗ = lim(t→∞)[−e^(−3t)/3 + 1/3] = 1/3, since e^(−3t) → 0.

3 multiplies by 3 instead of dividing; −1/3 keeps the minus that the lower limit cancels; the integral converges, because the exponential decays.
questions.concept: Improper integral of a decaying exponential

questions.q: The integrand of ∫₀⁹ (1/√x) dx is undefined at x = 0. Evaluate the integral.
questions.why:
The bad point is the lower limit, so ∫₀⁹x^(−1/2)dx = lim(c→0⁺)∫_c⁹x^(−1/2)dx = lim(c→0⁺)[2√x]_c⁹ = lim(c→0⁺)(6 − 2√c) = 6. It converges to 6.

3 forgets the factor 2 in the antiderivative 2√x; 18 integrates √x instead of 1/√x, giving (2/3)(27); the integral is not divergent, because 2√c tends to 0, not infinity.
questions.concept: Type II improper integral at the lower limit

questions.q: Determine ∫₀¹ x^(−3/2) dx.
questions.why:
The integrand blows up at x = 0, so take the one-sided limit: lim(c→0⁺)[−2x^(−1/2)]_c¹ = lim(c→0⁺)(−2 + 2/√c). Since 2/√c → +∞, the limit does not exist and the integral is divergent.

−2 substitutes 0 into −2x^(−1/2) as though it were finite; 2 does the same with the sign repaired; 2/3 uses the antiderivative for x^(−1/2) rather than x^(−3/2).
questions.concept: Type II improper integral that diverges

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ x²e^(−x) dx.
questions.why:
Integrating by parts twice gives the antiderivative −x²e^(−x) − 2xe^(−x) − 2e^(−x). At the upper limit each term tends to 0, since the exponential beats any power, and at x = 0 the value is −2. So the integral is 0 − (−2) = 2, and it converges.

0 assumes the whole antiderivative vanishes and forgets the lower limit; 1 is the value of ∫₀^∞xe^(−x)dx, one pass of parts too few; it does not diverge, because x²e^(−x) → 0.
questions.concept: Improper integral needing integration by parts twice

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₂^∞ 1/(x³ + 5x) dx converges or diverges.
questions.why:
For x ≥ 2, x³ + 5x ≥ x³, and taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the inequality, so 0 ≤ 1/(x³ + 5x) ≤ 1/x³. Take f(x) = 1/x³ and g(x) = 1/(x³ + 5x), so 0 ≤ g ≤ f. Since p = 3 > 1, ∫₂^∞dx/x³ converges, and the comparison test makes the smaller integral converge too.

Comparing with 1/x is the wrong bound here, and 1/x has p = 1, which diverges; a divergent verdict would need the given integrand to be the larger function, which it is not.
questions.concept: Comparison test, convergent direction

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₁^∞ (2 + sin(x))/x dx converges or diverges.
questions.why:
Since −1 ≤ sin(x) ≤ 1, the numerator satisfies 2 + sin(x) ≥ 1, so 0 ≤ 1/x ≤ (2 + sin(x))/x for x ≥ 1. Here g(x) = 1/x is the smaller function and ∫₁^∞dx/x diverges, because p = 1 sits on the divergent side of the p-test. By the comparison test the larger integral diverges too.

3/x is an upper bound, and a divergent upper bound proves nothing; 1/x² is smaller, and a convergent smaller function also proves nothing; 1/x³ is not a bound for this integrand at all.
questions.concept: Comparison test, divergent direction

questions.q: Which of these definite integrals is improper?
questions.why:
An integral is improper when a limit of integration is infinite or the integrand is discontinuous somewhere on the interval. In ∫₀²dx/(x − 1)² the integrand blows up at x = 1, which lies strictly inside [0, 2], so it is improper and must be split at x = 1.

1/(x − 2) is discontinuous only at x = 2, which is outside [0, 1]; 1/x³ is continuous on [1, 2]; √x is continuous on [0, 1], and a bounded integrand on a finite interval is an ordinary definite integral.
questions.concept: Recognising an improper integral

questions.q: For which values of p does ∫₁^∞ (1/xᵖ) dx converge?
questions.why:
The p-test says ∫₁^∞dx/xᵖ converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1. The boundary case p = 1 belongs to the divergent side, which is why ∫₁^∞dx/x diverges.

p ≥ 1 wrongly includes that boundary case; p < 1 and p ≤ 1 name exactly the values for which the integral diverges.
questions.concept: The p-test at infinity

questions.q: Find the area between the curve y = 4x − x² and the x-axis.
questions.why:
No interval is given, so the limits are the roots: 4x − x² = x(4 − x) = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 4. Test an interior point: at x = 2 the value is 8 − 4 = 4 > 0, so the curve is above the axis and no modulus is needed. A = ∫₀⁴(4x − x²)dx = [2x² − x³/3]₀⁴ = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3 square units.

16/3 stops the integral at x = 2; 32 keeps only the first term; 64/3 keeps only the second.
questions.concept: Area between a curve and the x-axis with roots as limits

questions.q: Find the area bounded by the curve y = x² − 4, the x-axis and the lines x = 0 and x = 3.
questions.why:
x² − 4 = 0 gives x = ±2, and x = 2 lies inside [0, 3], so the curve crosses there. With F(x) = x³/3 − 4x: on [0, 2] the curve is below the axis and that piece contributes |F(2) − F(0)| = |−16/3| = 16/3; on [2, 3] it is above and contributes F(3) − F(2) = −3 + 16/3 = 7/3. The area is 16/3 + 7/3 = 23/3 square units.

3 is the magnitude of the unsplit integral, in which the two pieces partly cancel; 16/3 and 7/3 are the separate pieces reported alone.
questions.concept: Splitting at a root where the curve crosses the axis

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed by the parabola y = x² and the line y = x + 6.
questions.why:
Solve x² = x + 6, that is x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, so the limits are x = −2 and x = 3. Test x = 0: the line gives 6 and the parabola gives 0, so the line is on top. A = ∫₋₂³[(x + 6) − x²]dx = [x²/2 + 6x − x³/3]₋₂³ = 27/2 − (−22/3) = 125/6 square units.

125/3 doubles the answer; 95/6 uses limits −3 and 2 from mis-factoring the quadratic; −125/6 subtracts in the wrong order, and an area is never negative.
questions.concept: Area enclosed by a line and a parabola

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curve y = 12 − x² and the line y = 3.
questions.why:
Solve 12 − x² = 3, so x² = 9 and the limits are x = −3 and x = 3. At x = 0 the curve gives 12 and the line gives 3, so the curve is on top. A = ∫₋₃³[(12 − x²) − 3]dx = ∫₋₃³(9 − x²)dx = [9x − x³/3]₋₃³ = 18 − (−18) = 36 square units.

18 uses only the half from 0 to 3; 54 forgets to subtract the line and integrates 12 − x²; 72 doubles the correct answer by counting both halves twice.
questions.concept: Area between a curve and a horizontal line

questions.q: Find the total area between the curves y = x and y = x³ from x = −1 to x = 1.
questions.why:
The curves meet where x = x³, that is at x = −1, 0 and 1, so x = 0 is an interior crossing and the integral must be split there. On [0, 1] the line is on top: ∫₀¹(x − x³)dx = 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4. On [−1, 0] the cubic is on top: ∫₋₁⁰(x³ − x)dx = 1/4. Total area = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 square units.

0 is the unsplit integral, in which the two congruent lobes cancel exactly; 1/4 reports one lobe only; 1 doubles the total.
questions.concept: Total area when two curves cross inside the interval

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed by y = √x and y = x².
questions.why:
Solve √x = x²: squaring gives x = x⁴, so x(x³ − 1) = 0 and the limits are x = 0 and x = 1. Test x = 1/4: √x = 0.5 and x² = 0.0625, so √x is on top. A = ∫₀¹(√x − x²)dx = [(2/3)x^(3/2) − x³/3]₀¹ = 2/3 − 1/3 = 1/3 square units.

2/3 integrates √x alone; 1/6 uses the line y = x in place of y = √x; −1/3 subtracts in the wrong order.
questions.concept: Area between two curves meeting at 0 and 1

questions.q: Find the area between y = sin(x) and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π.
questions.why:
sin(x) = 0 at x = π inside the interval, so split there. On [0, π] the curve is above the axis: ∫₀^π sin(x)dx = [−cos(x)]₀^π = 1 + 1 = 2. On [π, 2π] it is below, so take the modulus: |∫_π^(2π)sin(x)dx| = |−1 − 1| = 2. Total = 4 square units.

2 counts one arch only; 0 is the unsplit integral, where the two arches cancel; 2π confuses the width of the interval with the area.
questions.concept: Area where the curve dips below the axis

questions.q: Two curves cross once at x = c strictly inside [a, b], with f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, c] and g(x) ≥ f(x) on [c, b]. Which expression gives the total area between them on [a, b]?
questions.why:
Split at the crossing and write the top function first in each piece, so each integral is already positive: A = ∫ₐᶜ(f − g)dx + ∫ᶜᵇ(g − f)dx.

The single integral ∫ₐᵇ(f − g)dx lets the two pieces cancel and can even come out as 0; taking its modulus afterwards repairs nothing, because the cancellation has already happened; the last option is the sum of an integral and its own negative, which is always 0.
questions.concept: Area when curves cross inside the interval

questions.q: The region under y = 2x + 1, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why:
The axis is the x-axis, so the radius is R(x) = 2x + 1 and V = π∫₀¹(2x + 1)²dx = π∫₀¹(4x² + 4x + 1)dx = π[4x³/3 + 2x² + x]₀¹ = π(4/3 + 3) = 13π/3 cubic units.

2π forgets to square the radius; 7π/3 squares only the first term, using 4x² + 1; 13/3 drops the factor π.
questions.concept: Disc method about the x-axis

questions.q: The region under y = x², above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 2 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why:
Disc method with R(x) = x²: V = π∫₀²(x²)²dx = π∫₀²x⁴dx = π[x⁵/5]₀² = 32π/5 cubic units.

8π/3 integrates x² without squaring it; 8π uses the shell formula 2π∫x·x²dx, which is the volume of a different solid; 64π/5 doubles the correct value.
questions.concept: Disc method with a parabola

questions.q: The region between y = 4 and y = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why:
There is a hollow spot, so use washers. The outer boundary is the line y = 4, so R(x) = 4, and the inner boundary is the parabola, so r(x) = x². V = π∫₀²(16 − x⁴)dx = π[16x − x⁵/5]₀² = π(32 − 32/5) = 128π/5 cubic units.

256π/15 squares the difference, π∫(4 − x²)²dx, instead of subtracting the squares; 32π/5 is the inner solid alone; 8π uses the shell formula for a set-up that calls for washers.
questions.concept: Washer method about the x-axis

questions.q: The region under y = 4 − x², above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 2 is revolved about the y-axis. Use the shell method to find the volume.
questions.why:
The radius of a shell is its distance x from the y-axis and its height is f(x) = 4 − x², so V = 2π∫₀²x(4 − x²)dx = 2π∫₀²(4x − x³)dx = 2π[2x² − x⁴/4]₀² = 2π(8 − 4) = 8π cubic units.

4π drops the factor 2 in 2π; 256π/15 uses discs about the x-axis, a different solid; 16π doubles the answer by squaring the radius as well.
questions.concept: Shell method about the y-axis

questions.q: The region bounded by x = 2y², the y-axis and the line y = 1 is revolved about the y-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why:
The axis is the y-axis, so integrate in y with radius R(y) = 2y²: V = π∫₀¹(2y²)²dy = π∫₀¹4y⁴dy = π[4y⁵/5]₀¹ = 4π/5 cubic units.

2π/3 forgets to square, integrating 2y²; 2π/5 squares y² but not the coefficient 2; 8π/5 doubles the correct answer.
questions.concept: Disc method in y about the y-axis

questions.q: The region under y = x², above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 1 is revolved about the line y = 2. Find the volume.
questions.why:
Measure every radius from the line y = 2. The boundary farther from that line is y = 0, so R(x) = 2, and the nearer boundary is the curve, so r(x) = 2 − x². V = π∫₀¹[4 − (2 − x²)²]dx = π∫₀¹(4x² − x⁴)dx = π(4/3 − 1/5) = 17π/15 cubic units.

π/5 revolves about the x-axis and ignores the shift; 23π/15 uses R = x² + 2, which is the radius for the line y = −2; 43π/15 forgets to subtract the inner radius and takes π∫(2 − x²)²dx.
questions.concept: Washer method about a horizontal line other than the x-axis

questions.q: The region between y = 2x and y = x² is revolved about the y-axis. Use the shell method to find the volume.
questions.why:
Solve 2x = x² for the limits: x(2 − x) = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 2. On (0, 2) the line is above the parabola, so the strip height is 2x − x² and the radius is x. V = 2π∫₀²x(2x − x²)dx = 2π∫₀²(2x² − x³)dx = 2π[2x³/3 − x⁴/4]₀² = 2π(16/3 − 4) = 8π/3 cubic units.

4π/3 uses π instead of 2π; 64π/15 revolves about the x-axis with washers; 16π/3 doubles the answer.
questions.concept: Shell method with a region between two curves

questions.q: A washer has outer radius R and inner radius r. Which expression gives the area of its face?
questions.why:
The face is a full disc of radius R with a disc of radius r removed, so its area is πR² − πr². That is why the washer formula reads V = π∫([R]² − [r]²)dx, with the squares subtracted.

π(R − r)² subtracts the radii before squaring, which gives a smaller number and a different solid; 2π(R − r) is a length times 2π, not an area; π(R² + r²) adds the two discs instead of removing one.
questions.concept: Area of a washer cross-section

questions.q: A body moves with velocity v(t) = 8t − 2 m/s. Find its net displacement between t = 1 s and t = 4 s.
questions.why:
Net displacement is the integral of velocity: ∫₁⁴(8t − 2)dt = [4t² − 2t]₁⁴ = (64 − 8) − (4 − 2) = 56 − 2 = 54 m.

56 m forgets to subtract the value at the lower limit; 30 m is v(4), the speed at the end rather than the distance covered; 58 m adds the lower value instead of subtracting it.
questions.concept: Net displacement as the integral of velocity

questions.q: A firm's marginal revenue is MR(Q) = 50 + 6Q, and its total revenue at Q = 3 is 200. Find the total revenue function TR(Q).
questions.why:
TR(Q) = ∫MR(Q)dQ = 50Q + 3Q² + C. Now solve for C using the data point: TR(3) = 150 + 27 + C = 177 + C, and 177 + C = 200 gives C = 23. So TR(Q) = 50Q + 3Q² + 23.

+200 copies the given revenue straight into C instead of solving an equation; 6Q² fails to divide 6 by the new power 2; −23 mishandles the sign when 177 is moved across.
questions.concept: Recovering total revenue from marginal revenue

questions.q: A rectangular dam face is 20 m high and 50 m wide, with its top level with the water surface. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 m/s². Find the total fluid force on the face.
questions.why:
The weight density is w = ρg = 9800 N/m³, the depth of the strip at position x is h(x) = x and the width is L(x) = 50. So F = ∫₀²⁰(9800)(x)(50)dx = 490000[x²/2]₀²⁰ = 490000 × 200 = 9.8 × 10⁷ N.

1.96 × 10⁸ N forgets to divide by 2 in [x²/2]; 1.0 × 10⁷ N uses ρ = 1000 alone and leaves out g; 9.8 × 10⁴ N uses g = 9.8 alone and leaves out ρ.
questions.concept: Fluid force on a vertical rectangular face

questions.q: A 30 m rope of mass 500 g/m hangs over the edge of a cliff. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the work done in pulling the whole rope to the top.
questions.why:
Convert first: 500 g/m = 0.5 kg/m. After x metres have been pulled up, (30 − x) m still hangs, with mass 0.5(30 − x) kg and weight F(x) = 9.8(0.5)(30 − x) = 4.9(30 − x) N. So W = ∫₀³⁰4.9(30 − x)dx = 4.9[30x − x²/2]₀³⁰ = 4.9(900 − 450) = 2205 J.

4410 J treats the force as constant at its starting value and uses W = F × d; 2 205 000 J leaves the mass in grams; 1102.5 J halves the correct answer.
questions.concept: Work done by a variable force

questions.q: The rate of investment is I(t) = 9√t. Find the capital growth between the 1st and the 4th years.
questions.why:
Rewrite the root as a power: K = ∫₁⁴9t^(1/2)dt = 9·t^(3/2)/(3/2) = 6t^(3/2), evaluated from 1 to 4. Since 4^(3/2) = 8 and 1^(3/2) = 1, K = 6(8) − 6(1) = 48 − 6 = 42.

63 uses 9t^(3/2) without dividing by 3/2; 9 computes I(4) − I(1), substituting into the rate instead of the antiderivative; 94.5 multiplies by 3/2 instead of dividing.
questions.concept: Capital growth from a rate of investment

questions.q: For a product the demand function is D(Q) = 100 − 2Q and the supply function is S(Q) = 20 + Q². Find the equilibrium quantity Q₀ and the consumer surplus.
questions.why:
Set D(Q) = S(Q): 100 − 2Q = 20 + Q² gives Q² + 2Q − 80 = 0, so (Q + 10)(Q − 8) = 0 and the positive root is Q₀ = 8. Then P₀ = D(8) = 100 − 16 = 84. CS = ∫₀⁸[D(Q) − P₀]dQ = ∫₀⁸(16 − 2Q)dQ = [16Q − Q²]₀⁸ = 128 − 64 = 64.

CS = 128 drops the −2Q term and integrates the constant 16 alone; Q₀ = 10 takes the negative root −10 without its sign; CS ≈ 341.3 is the producer surplus ∫₀⁸(64 − Q²)dQ, not the consumer surplus.
questions.concept: Equilibrium and consumer surplus

questions.q: A resource is consumed at the rate 24e^(0.04t) thousand tonnes per year, t years from now, and nothing has been consumed at t = 0. After how many years does the total consumed reach 900 thousand tonnes?
questions.why:
Integrate the rate: C(t) = ∫24e^(0.04t)dt = (24/0.04)e^(0.04t) + c = 600e^(0.04t) + c. The condition C(0) = 0 gives 0 = 600 + c, so c = −600 and C(t) = 600e^(0.04t) − 600. Setting C(t) = 900 gives e^(0.04t) = 2.5, so t = ln(2.5)/0.04 ≈ 22.9 years.

10.1 years forgets the −600 and solves 600e^(0.04t) = 900; 2.3 years divides the logarithm by 0.4; 229 years divides it by 0.004.
questions.concept: Solving an exponential accumulation model for time

questions.q: A body's velocity is v(t) and its displacement is x(t) = ∫v(t)dt = F(t) + C. Which single piece of information fixes C?
options: The displacement at one known time, such as x(0)
questions.why:
C shifts the whole displacement function up or down, so one known position pins it: substituting a known x(t₀) into F(t₀) + C gives an equation with C as the only unknown. With x(0) it is especially quick, because F(0) is usually 0 and C = x(0).

The velocity at t = 0 is the integrand's value and says nothing about where the body started; the acceleration is v′(t), one derivative further away still; the total distance is a length, not a position, and any C gives the same distance because the constant cancels in every difference.
questions.concept: Fixing the constant of integration from an initial condition
